newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan rules out cut in defence budget.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan rules out cut in defence budget.

text.p: The defence minister of Pakistan's caretaker government said on Thursday that Islamabad would not slash its defence budget despite its economic woes as long it faced a security threat.

Shahid Hamid also told a news conference that the controversial Council for Defence and National Security created by President Farooq Leghari does not mean the military will be involved in politics as claimed by the body's critics.

The controversial body gives the military a formal advisory role in government affairs. Its members include the chiefs of armed forces, along with the president, prime minister and some key ministers.

Asked if the military leaders in the council would make it difficult for any political government to cut Pakistan's heavy defence budget, Hamid said: "We are not going to take any step to cut the defence budget given the current security threat."
He seemed to be referring to the military threat Pakistan has felt from arch rival India.
The two neighbours have fought three wars, two of them over the disputed Himalayan region of Kashmir, since gaining independence from Britain in 1947.

Hamid said the advice of the top military brass on economic matters relating to defence was necessary because the armed forces consumed more than a quarter of the national budget, or six percent of the gross domestic product.

Hamid said Leghari formed the council on Monday, less than a month before new elections set for February 3, to formalise an arrangement of consultation with the military that already existed informally.

Ousted Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, who was dismissed by Leghari on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, has accused the president of trying to drag the armed forces into politics to bolster himself.
"Nothing of the sort," said Hamid, a close confidant of Leghari.
"Everybody acknowledges that the armed forces are neutral... and will remain neutral."
Government spokesmen say the council's advice will not be binding and it will not supersede the powers of the prime ministerial cabinet.

But its critics say it will be hard for any political government to say no to the advice from the leaders of the military, which has ruled Pakistan for about half of its existence since its creation in 1947 from the partition of the Indian sub-continent.
